title: Early mean event distance gave no clear later-count forecast gain after 323 shallow M6.5+ earthquakes in 2013-2024
abstract: We tested whether mean distance of nearby events on days 1-7 improves forecasts of event counts on days 7-30. We used a fixed global ComCat M5.5+ snapshot. Centers had preferred magnitude at least 6.5 and depth at most 70 km. Fits used 363 centers in 2001-2012; tests used 323 centers in 2013-2024. The reference model used center magnitude and depth, early count, early largest magnitude, an early-event indicator, and prior local count. Adding mean early distance within 200 km reduced mean test Poisson deviance by 0.000331, or 0.0202%. The conditional 95% three-year block interval was -0.001519 to 0.002251. All planned radius and first-day checks also gave intervals that included zero. Only 81 test centers had an early event in the primary window. This test gives no clear support for the added distance term. It does not rule out spatial effects or show equal practical performance. Sparse early counts, simple model form, revised records, shared windows and twelve test years limit inference. Code, source hashes, aggregate evidence, uncertainty draws, checks and a figure are supplied. Source records and event-level tables remain external.

display.caption: Adding early mean event distance gave no clear later-count gain. Positive deviance reduction favors the added term. Bars are conditional 95% three-year block intervals. All four intervals include zero.

citations.reason: We extend its time-split count forecast design with an early distance feature and additional reference terms. The source and centers overlap; this is not independent replication.
Its spatial-share test motivates control for prior local counts. The source overlaps.
